Jeremiah 1.summary: The LORD calls Jeremiah before his birth and appoints him a prophet to the nations, though he protests that he is too young to speak (Jeremiah 1:4-10). God touches his mouth, promises him the words to speak, and shows him an almond branch and a boiling pot tilted from the north, signs of judgment advancing on Judah for its own wrongdoing (Jeremiah 1:11-16). God warns that Jeremiah will face fierce resistance, yet promises to make him as unbreakable as a fortified city and a bronze wall (Jeremiah 1:17-19).
Jeremiah 1.whereWeAre: Isaiah's final chapters pictured nations gathered to witness God's glory even as idolatry still faced judgment. Jeremiah opens very differently: a young priest's son from Anathoth is called before his birth to be a prophet to the nations, right as Judah's last kings begin their decline. Chapter 2 opens his first extended message, recalling Israel's youthful devotion before indicting the present generation's unfaithfulness.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: A young priest's son from Anathoth, appointed a prophet to the nations before his birth despite protesting that he is too young to speak (1:4-7).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Touches Jeremiah's mouth, puts his own words in the prophet's mouth, and shows him the almond branch and the tilted boiling pot that explain the coming judgment (1:9-14).

keyFigures.name: the people and kings of Judah
keyFigures.role: The addressees of the coming judgment, warned that they will fight against Jeremiah but will not prevail because God is with him (1:18-19).

keyThemes.explanation: God appoints Jeremiah a prophet before his birth and overrules his protest that he is too young, showing that the call rests on God's choice rather than the prophet's own readiness (1:4-8).
The boiling pot tilted from the north previews an invasion that will fall on Judah because of its own wrongdoing, not merely because a foreign army happens to attack (1:13-16).
God promises to make Jeremiah as unbreakable as a fortified city and an iron pillar so that fierce opposition cannot silence his message (1:17-19).

Jeremiah 2.summary: God recalls Israel's early devotion in the wilderness and charges Judah with abandoning the fountain of living water for broken, useless cisterns (Jeremiah 2:1-13). The chapter names devotion to other gods and political dependence on Egypt and Assyria as the same underlying betrayal (Jeremiah 2:14-19). Judah denies any wrongdoing despite the charges, even as God insists the evidence of its unfaithfulness is plain (Jeremiah 2:20-37).
Jeremiah 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 ended with Jeremiah commissioned and warned that Judah itself, not just a foreign army, would resist his message. Here his first message begins: God recalls Israel's early devotion in the wilderness and charges Judah with trading the fountain of living water for broken cisterns and foreign alliances. Chapter 3 continues the charge, comparing Judah's unfaithfulness to a formal divorce and inviting the backsliding nation to return.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Recalls Israel's early devotion in the wilderness and accuses Judah of trading the fountain of living water for broken cisterns and foreign alliances (2:2-13).

keyFigures.name: Jerusalem and Judah
keyFigures.role: Accused of abandoning God for idols and for political dependence on Egypt and Assyria, yet denies any wrongdoing despite the evidence (2:23-35).

keyFigures.name: Egypt and Assyria
keyFigures.role: The foreign powers Judah courts for protection instead of trusting God, pictured as the waters of the Nile and the Euphrates (2:18, 2:36).

keyThemes.explanation: God remembers Israel's bridal devotion in the wilderness, making its present unfaithfulness feel like the loss of a real, personal relationship rather than a broken rule (2:2-3).
Trusting Egypt and Assyria is treated as the same basic failure as worshiping idols, since both put confidence in something other than God (2:18, 2:36-37).
Judah insists it has not sinned even as God lists specific, visible evidence against it, showing how denial can coexist with obvious guilt (2:23, 2:35).

Jeremiah 3.summary: Jeremiah compares Judah and Israel's unfaithfulness to a wife worse than her own divorced sister, recalling the northern kingdom's earlier downfall (Jeremiah 3:1-11). He nevertheless calls the people to return and confess their guilt, promising shepherds after God's own heart (Jeremiah 3:12-15). The chapter closes picturing a future gathering of the nations to Jerusalem and a reunited Israel and Judah coming home together (Jeremiah 3:16-18).
Jeremiah 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 charged Judah with abandoning God for idols and foreign powers. Here Jeremiah compares Judah to a wife worse than her already-divorced sister, the northern kingdom, yet still invites both to return and promises shepherds after God's own heart. Chapter 4 answers that invitation with a demand for sincere repentance before shifting to an urgent alarm of invasion.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Compares Judah and Israel's unfaithfulness to a wife worse than her divorced sister, yet still invites both to return and confess their guilt (3:1-14).

keyFigures.name: faithless Israel
keyFigures.role: The northern kingdom, already judged and exiled by Assyria, held up as a warning example for Judah (3:6-10).

keyFigures.name: treacherous Judah
keyFigures.role: Judah itself, shown to have ignored Israel's example and sinned even more openly through false repentance (3:10-11).

keyFigures.name: Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: Promised a future where it is called the LORD's throne and nations gather to it, if the invitation to return is accepted (3:17).

keyThemes.explanation: Despite the harsh comparison, God still calls Judah to simply acknowledge its guilt and return, keeping the door open even after everything said before (3:12-14).
Judah is measured against the northern kingdom's earlier fall, exposing it as worse because it saw Israel's judgment and sinned anyway (3:6-11).
The promise of future shepherds and a city without need for the ark pictures worship renewed from the heart rather than centered on an object (3:15-17).

Jeremiah 4.summary: Jeremiah calls Israel and Judah to a genuine return marked by justice and renewed hearts, not empty ritual (Jeremiah 4:1-4). The tone then breaks into urgent alarm as a destroyer from the north advances toward Jerusalem, sounded by trumpets and watched for in fortified towns (Jeremiah 4:5-18). Jeremiah pictures the devastation in the language of creation undone, grieving a disaster he cannot escape even as he announces it (Jeremiah 4:19-31).
Jeremiah 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 invited Judah to return with a sincere heart. Here Jeremiah first presses that same call to genuine repentance, then the tone breaks into urgent alarm: a destroyer from the north is coming, and the prophet pictures the land itself undone like the darkness before creation. Chapter 5 continues the indictment, as God sends Jeremiah searching Jerusalem's streets for even one honest person.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Calls Israel and Judah to genuine repentance marked by justice and renewed hearts, then warns of an invading army from the north (4:1-6).

keyFigures.name: Judah and Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: The target of the coming invasion, urged to sound the alarm and gather into fortified cities before the destroyer arrives (4:5-8).

keyFigures.name: the northern invader
keyFigures.role: An unnamed army compared to a lion and an eagle, advancing on Jerusalem as the specific instrument of judgment (4:7, 4:13).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Caught between delivering the warning and his own grief, crying out in anguish at the devastation he foresees (4:19-21).

keyThemes.explanation: God calls for circumcised hearts, not just outward ritual, insisting that real repentance has to reach beneath the surface (4:1-4).
Trumpets, signal flags, and a lion from the thicket build a mounting sense of danger that Jerusalem cannot ignore or outrun (4:5-7).
Jeremiah's vision of the earth 'without form, and void' borrows creation's own language to show how total this coming devastation will feel (4:23).

Jeremiah 5.summary: God challenges Jeremiah to search Jerusalem for even one person who practices justice and truth, and he finds none among the poor or the powerful (Jeremiah 5:1-9). Leaders and ordinary people alike are accused of rejecting correction and exploiting the vulnerable for their own gain (Jeremiah 5:10-31). A powerful foreign nation is announced as the agent of coming judgment, though the chapter insists that Judah's ruin will not be absolute (Jeremiah 5:15-19).
Jeremiah 5.whereWeAre: Chapter 4 raised the alarm over an invader from the north. Here God sends Jeremiah through Jerusalem's streets to find even one person who does justly, and finds none among rich or poor, while a powerful nation is announced as the instrument of judgment. Chapter 6 continues the siege warning, naming the approaching army and the leaders who falsely promise peace.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends Jeremiah through Jerusalem's streets to find even one person who practices justice, and finds none among rich or poor (5:1-5).

keyFigures.name: Jerusalem's residents and leaders
keyFigures.role: Accused of rejecting correction, growing fat and sleek through oppression, and defending the cause of the fatherless unjustly (5:26-28).

keyFigures.name: foreign nation
keyFigures.role: An unnamed but powerful people summoned from far away as the agent of coming judgment (5:15-17).

keyFigures.name: prophets and priests
keyFigures.role: Condemned for prophesying falsely and ruling by their own means while the people love having it so (5:30-31).

keyThemes.explanation: The search for even one honest person in Jerusalem turns a general accusation into a specific, almost forensic indictment of the whole city (5:1-5).
Refusing correction and hardening their faces harder than rock is named as the direct cause of the disaster about to fall (5:3, 5:19).
Becoming fat and sleek through oppressing orphans and the poor shows that Judah's sin is social and economic, not only religious (5:27-28).

Jeremiah 6.summary: An invading army threatens Jerusalem from the north, and the people are urged to seek the ancient paths while there is still time (Jeremiah 6:1-16). They refuse the warning, and leaders offer false reassurances of peace even as disaster nears (Jeremiah 6:13-15). The chapter closes comparing the people to silver that refining cannot purify, rejected because their corruption runs too deep to remove (Jeremiah 6:27-30).
Jeremiah 6.whereWeAre: Chapter 5 found no one in Jerusalem practicing justice. Here the invading army draws closer: trumpets sound the alarm, leaders offer false reassurances of peace, and the chapter closes picturing the people as rejected silver that refining cannot purify. Chapter 7 moves the warning to the temple gate itself, as Jeremiah confronts worshipers trusting the building rather than God.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Warns of an invading army from the north and calls the people to seek the ancient, good paths before it is too late (6:1, 6:16).

keyFigures.name: people of Benjamin and Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: Urged to flee and sound the alarm as the besieging army closes in on the city (6:1).

keyFigures.name: prophets and priests
keyFigures.role: Offer false reassurance, saying 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace at all (6:13-14).

keyFigures.name: invading army
keyFigures.role: A besieging force pictured cutting down trees and building siege mounds against Jerusalem itself (6:4-6).

keyThemes.explanation: Being told to seek the good, old paths and refusing outright shows a people who reject guidance even when it is freely offered (6:16-17).
Saying 'Peace, peace' when there is no peace names a specific kind of leadership failure: comforting people instead of warning them honestly (6:14).
Jeremiah is cast as a tester of metal whose people turn out to be rejected silver, too corrupted for refining to purify (6:27-30).

Jeremiah 7.summary: At the temple gate, Jeremiah warns worshipers not to trust the sanctuary itself as a guarantee of safety while they steal, murder, and serve other gods (Jeremiah 7:1-11). He demands justice for immigrants, orphans, and widows, and recalls Shiloh's ruin as proof that no sanctuary is beyond judgment (Jeremiah 7:5-15). The message condemns child sacrifice at Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom and foresees devastation for a people who will not change (Jeremiah 7:29-34).
Jeremiah 7.whereWeAre: Chapter 6 closed comparing the people to metal that refining cannot purify. Here Jeremiah stands at the gate of the LORD's house and warns worshipers that the temple is no guarantee of safety, recalling the ruined sanctuary at Shiloh and condemning child sacrifice at Topheth. Chapter 8 continues this temple sermon's themes of judgment and grief, mourning a people who refuse to turn back.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Sent to stand at the temple gate and warn worshipers that the sanctuary cannot protect those who steal, murder, and serve idols (7:1-11).

keyFigures.name: temple worshipers
keyFigures.role: Trust the phrase 'The temple of the LORD' as a guarantee of safety regardless of how they live (7:4, 7:9-10).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Recalls Shiloh's destruction as proof no sanctuary is exempt from judgment and forbids Jeremiah even to pray for this people (7:12-16).

keyFigures.name: Judah's rulers and people
keyFigures.role: Condemned for baking cakes to the 'queen of heaven' and sacrificing children at Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom (7:18, 7:31).

keyThemes.explanation: Repeating 'The temple of the LORD' three times exposes a superstition that treats God's house as a magic charm rather than a place that requires faithful living (7:4).
Justice for the stranger, orphan, and widow is named as a condition for staying in the land, not an optional extra to religious practice (7:5-7).
Child sacrifice at Topheth is condemned as something God never commanded and never even imagined, ruling out any claim that it served him (7:31).

explainedReferences.explanation: Phrase describing the temple as a den of thieves.
Phrase describing the temple as a den of thieves.
The phrase 'den of thieves' concerning the temple.

Jeremiah 8.summary: Judgment is pictured through the humiliation of disturbed graves and a people who refuse every chance to repent (Jeremiah 8:1-7). Scribes and religious leaders wrongly claim wisdom while treating the nation's wound as a light thing (Jeremiah 8:8-12). Jeremiah grieves for his people, asking why no healing has come though a balm is available in Gilead (Jeremiah 8:18-22).
Jeremiah 8.whereWeAre: Chapter 7 warned that the temple could not shield a disobedient people from judgment. Here that judgment is pictured as the disgrace of disturbed graves and a wound no one will heal, as Jeremiah grieves that scribes and leaders claim wisdom they do not have. Chapter 9 continues the lament, as Jeremiah longs to weep without ceasing for his people.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Pictures coming judgment as the disgrace of disturbed graves and condemns leaders who treat the nation's wound lightly (8:1-2, 8:11).

keyFigures.name: Judah's people
keyFigures.role: Refuse to turn back even though the time for repentance has already passed like a finished harvest (8:4-7, 8:20).

keyFigures.name: scribes and prophets
keyFigures.role: Wrongly claim wisdom through 'the pen of the scribes' while offering false assurances of peace (8:8-11).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Grieves for his people, asking why no healing has come though a balm is available in Gilead (8:18-22).

keyThemes.explanation: Even migrating birds know their appointed seasons, but Jeremiah says his people do not know the LORD's ordained time to repent (8:7).
Scribes who handle the law 'falsely' with their pens show that religious expertise can become a tool for deception rather than truth (8:8).
Jeremiah's grief over his people's wound, expressed as his own personal sorrow, shows that pronouncing judgment does not require losing compassion for those judged (8:21-22).

Jeremiah 9.summary: Jeremiah longs for tears enough to weep without ceasing over the deceit and violence filling his nation (Jeremiah 9:1-9). God announces judgment and instructs professional mourners to lament for what is coming (Jeremiah 9:10-22). The chapter rejects boasting in wisdom, strength, or wealth and commends instead knowing God's justice, mercy, and righteousness (Jeremiah 9:23-26).
Jeremiah 9.whereWeAre: Chapter 8 ended with Jeremiah asking why no healing has come to his people. Here he wishes for tears enough to weep day and night over their slain, while God instructs trained mourners to lament and redirects true boasting away from wisdom, strength, and wealth toward knowing God. Chapter 10 turns from this lament to a direct contrast between handmade idols and the living God.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Longs for tears enough to weep day and night over the slain of his people and their deceitful conduct (9:1-9).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Announces judgment and instructs trained mourners to lament, then redirects true boasting toward knowing him rather than wisdom, strength, or wealth (9:17-24).

keyFigures.name: people of Judah
keyFigures.role: Accused of deceit so constant that neighbor cannot trust neighbor, and of being circumcised in body but not in heart (9:4-6, 9:25-26).

keyFigures.name: women called to mourn
keyFigures.role: Professional mourners summoned to teach their daughters a wailing lament for the coming disaster (9:17-20).

keyThemes.explanation: Jeremiah wishes for a traveler's lodge in the wilderness so he could leave his own people, showing how deeply their sin wears him down (9:2).
Wisdom, might, and riches are each named and each rejected as a worthy basis for pride, leaving only knowing God as something worth boasting in (9:23-24).
Being circumcised in body but not in heart argues that a religious mark without a changed life accomplishes nothing (9:25-26).

explainedReferences.explanation: The instruction that anyone boasting should boast in the Lord.
That whoever boasts should boast in the Lord.

Jeremiah 10.summary: The chapter contrasts idols shaped by craftsmen, unable to speak or move, with the living God who made the heavens and earth (Jeremiah 10:1-16). It turns to warn of coming exile, picturing tents suddenly struck and children scattered (Jeremiah 10:17-22). Jeremiah closes with a humble, communal prayer asking for correction in just measure rather than complete destruction (Jeremiah 10:23-25).
Jeremiah 10.whereWeAre: Chapter 9 redirected true boasting toward knowing the LORD rather than wisdom, strength, or wealth. Here that contrast sharpens: idols shaped by craftsmen are mocked as lifeless, while the LORD is praised as maker of heaven and earth, before a warning of coming exile and a prayer pleading for correction rather than destruction. Chapter 11 turns to Judah's own broken promises, as Jeremiah proclaims the terms of the covenant it has forsaken.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Contrasted with lifeless idols as the living God who made the heavens and earth and controls the rain and the wind (10:10-13).

keyFigures.name: Judah and Israel
keyFigures.role: Warned of coming exile pictured as a tent suddenly struck, even as Jeremiah prays on their behalf for just correction (10:17-20, 10:24).

keyFigures.name: idol makers
keyFigures.role: Craftsmen whose handmade gods must be carried because they cannot walk, exposed as futile compared to the true God (10:3-5, 10:9).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Confesses that the way of man is not in himself and prays for correction in just measure rather than full destruction (10:23-25).

keyThemes.explanation: Idols that must be nailed down so they cannot topple over are set against the living God who made the earth and controls the weather (10:4-5, 10:12-13).
Jeremiah's admission that 'the way of man is not in himself' concedes that people cannot even direct their own steps, let alone escape judgment on their own (10:23).
The image of a tent suddenly taken down pictures exile as abrupt and disorienting rather than a slow, foreseeable decline (10:20).

Jeremiah 11.summary: Jeremiah proclaims the terms of the covenant and warns that its curses have come into view because of persistent disobedience (Jeremiah 11:1-8). God tells him not to intercede for the people, since their idolatry has multiplied as fast as their cities (Jeremiah 11:11-17). Jeremiah then learns that the men of his own hometown, Anathoth, are plotting to kill him for his message (Jeremiah 11:18-23).
Jeremiah 11.whereWeAre: Chapter 10 closed with a prayer pleading for correction rather than full destruction. Here Jeremiah proclaims the covenant's words and its curses for disobedience, then learns that the men of his own hometown, Anathoth, are plotting to kill him for it. Chapter 12 continues with Jeremiah's protest over that betrayal and his larger question of why the wicked prosper.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Proclaims the covenant's terms and its curses, and tells Jeremiah not to intercede because the people's idolatry has multiplied with their cities (11:1-8, 11:13-14).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Proclaims the covenant obediently, then discovers a plot on his own life, comparing himself to an unsuspecting lamb led to slaughter (11:6, 11:19).

keyFigures.name: men of Anathoth
keyFigures.role: Jeremiah's own hometown neighbors, who plot to kill him so he will stop prophesying (11:19-21).

keyFigures.name: Judah and Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: The covenant community whose disobedience has brought the curses written in the law into present reality (11:9-10).

keyThemes.explanation: Reciting the covenant's blessings and curses reminds Judah that the coming judgment was agreed to by their own ancestors, not imposed without warning (11:3-5).
God refuses to listen when the people cry out in trouble, since they ran after other gods just as numerous as their own cities in the meantime (11:11-13).
A plot from Jeremiah's own hometown shows that rejection of God's word can come from the people closest to the messenger, not just distant enemies (11:19-21).

Jeremiah 12.summary: Jeremiah asks God why the wicked prosper and why the whole land suffers for their wrongdoing (Jeremiah 12:1-4). God's answer is demanding rather than comforting, warning Jeremiah that harder trials, pictured as running with horses, still lie ahead (Jeremiah 12:5-6). The chapter closes addressing Judah's neighboring nations, promising their removal from the land but also a conditional future inclusion if they learn God's ways (Jeremiah 12:14-17).
Jeremiah 12.whereWeAre: Chapter 11 ended with a plot against Jeremiah's life from his own townspeople. Here he presses that painful experience into a larger question, asking why the wicked prosper, and receives a demanding answer about harder trials still to come, alongside a conditional promise for Judah's neighboring peoples. Chapter 13 turns from questions to a dramatized sign: a ruined linen girdle acting out Judah's ruined pride.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Asks God why the wicked prosper and the land itself suffers for their wrongdoing (12:1-4).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Answers with a demanding image of running against horses, warning that harder trials still lie ahead before compassion follows (12:5-6, 12:15).

keyFigures.name: Judah's wicked
keyFigures.role: Planted by God yet bearing no good fruit, their own betrayal reaching even into Jeremiah's family (12:2, 12:6).

keyFigures.name: neighboring peoples
keyFigures.role: Promised removal from the land for evil, but also a conditional future inclusion if they learn to swear by the LORD's name (12:14-16).

keyThemes.explanation: Jeremiah's blunt question about why the wicked prosper gives permission to voice real doubt about fairness rather than suppress it (12:1).
Being asked how he will keep up with horses if he is already worn out by footmen warns that present difficulty is not yet the hardest test (12:5).
Even the neighboring nations removed from their land are told they can be built up again if they learn to swear by the LORD's name (12:14-16).

Jeremiah 13.summary: Jeremiah buries a linen girdle near the Euphrates and later finds it ruined, a sign of Judah's pride spoiled by its own stubbornness (Jeremiah 13:1-11). A wine-jar saying announces coming disorientation, picturing a nation stumbling as if drunk (Jeremiah 13:12-14). Judah is summoned to humility before its glory is darkened, while Jerusalem's coming shame is described in deliberately disturbing terms of exposure (Jeremiah 13:15-27).
Jeremiah 13.whereWeAre: Chapter 12 ended with neighboring nations conditionally promised inclusion if they learn God's ways. Here Jeremiah acts out Judah's own fate instead: a linen girdle buried and later found rotten pictures ruined pride, followed by a wine-jar saying and a vivid warning of Jerusalem's coming shame. Chapter 14 turns to a different kind of national distress: a severe drought testing the land.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Buries a linen girdle near the Euphrates and later finds it ruined, acting out Judah's pride spoiled by its own stubbornness (13:1-11).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Explains the ruined girdle, warns through a wine-jar saying, and pictures Jerusalem's coming shame in deliberately disturbing terms (13:12-14, 13:22-27).

keyFigures.name: Judah and Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: Summoned to humility before their glory is darkened on the mountains, after stubbornly refusing correction (13:15-17).

keyFigures.name: king and queen mother
keyFigures.role: Told to take a lowly seat, since their glorious crowns are about to come down (13:18).

keyThemes.explanation: A linen girdle, once close to the body, ruined by being buried and forgotten, pictures how intimacy with God becomes worthless when neglected (13:9-11).
Judah is told to give glory to God before darkness falls, since pride left unchecked will not get a second chance once judgment arrives (13:16).
Judah's habits are called as fixed as a leopard's spots, meaning change will have to come from outside since it clearly will not come from within (13:23).

Jeremiah 14.summary: A severe drought dries up Judah's cisterns and fields, leaving even wild animals to suffer (Jeremiah 14:1-6). The people confess their wrongdoing and plead for mercy, but God condemns prophets who promise peace without his authorization (Jeremiah 14:7-16). Jeremiah laments the combined suffering of sword, famine, and religious deception sweeping over the land (Jeremiah 14:17-22).
Jeremiah 14.whereWeAre: Chapter 13 pictured Judah's pride ruined like a spoiled linen girdle. Here a severe drought tests the land instead, and the people's confession of sin is met not with relief but with God's refusal of prophets who promise peace without his authorization. Chapter 15 continues this refusal, declaring that not even Moses or Samuel could now turn judgment aside.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Describes the drought ravaging Judah, then refuses the prophets of peace, declaring that sword, famine, and plague are his true sentence (14:1-6, 14:13-16).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Laments the suffering of sword and famine and pleads with God on behalf of the very people under judgment (14:17-22).

keyFigures.name: Judah's people
keyFigures.role: Confess their wrongdoing and plead for mercy during the drought, invoking God's name even while continuing to sin (14:7-9, 14:20-21).

keyFigures.name: false prophets
keyFigures.role: Promise peace and prosperity without God's authorization, a claim God condemns outright (14:13-15).

keyThemes.explanation: Nursing deer abandoning their young and wild donkeys panting for water show that the drought's judgment touches even creatures that never sinned (14:5-6).
The people's honest confession of guilt is met not with automatic relief but with God's continued refusal to turn judgment aside (14:7, 14:10).
Prophets promising 'ye shall not see the sword' are condemned for speaking a vision God never gave them (14:13-14).

Jeremiah 15.summary: God announces that even famous intercessors like Moses and Samuel could not now avert the coming judgment, because of what Manasseh did in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 15:1-9). Jeremiah protests the weight of his calling, accusing God of making him a man of strife to the whole earth (Jeremiah 15:10-18). God answers with a renewed commission, promising to make Jeremiah a fortified bronze wall if he keeps speaking faithfully (Jeremiah 15:19-21).
Jeremiah 15.whereWeAre: Chapter 14 showed God rejecting prophets who promised peace during the drought. Here that refusal is stated even more starkly: not even Moses or Samuel's intercession could turn judgment away, before the chapter turns inward to Jeremiah's own raw protest and his renewed commission to keep speaking God's words. Chapter 16 continues this personal cost, as Jeremiah's own life becomes a sign of the judgment he proclaims.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Declares that not even Moses or Samuel could now turn judgment away, naming Manasseh's past sins as a reason, before renewing Jeremiah's own commission (15:1-4, 15:19-21).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Protests the weight of his calling as a man of strife to the whole earth, yet still delights in God's word as his heart's joy (15:10, 15:16).

keyFigures.name: Moses and Samuel
keyFigures.role: Israel's great past intercessors, invoked as a measure of how fixed this judgment now is (15:1).

keyFigures.name: Judah
keyFigures.role: Appointed to four kinds of destruction, sword, dogs, birds, and beasts, because of what happened in Manasseh's Jerusalem (15:2-4).

keyThemes.explanation: Naming Moses and Samuel, Israel's greatest intercessors, as powerless to help now shows how far beyond ordinary pleading this judgment has gone (15:1).
Jeremiah's complaint that he sits alone under God's hand pictures the real loneliness that can come with faithfully delivering an unwelcome message (15:17).
Being told to return to God rather than let God return to him puts the responsibility for restoration back on Jeremiah even in his distress (15:19).

Jeremiah 16.summary: Jeremiah is told not to marry, mourn, or feast, so that his own restricted life becomes a visible sign of the catastrophe coming on Judah's families (Jeremiah 16:1-9). Persistent idolatry is named as the reason exile is coming, generations deep and inherited from the fathers (Jeremiah 16:10-13). Yet the chapter still promises a future regathering so complete it will eclipse even the memory of the exodus from Egypt (Jeremiah 16:14-21).
Jeremiah 16.whereWeAre: Chapter 15 ended with Jeremiah's vocation renewed despite his anguish. Here that vocation reshapes his daily life: he is told not to marry, mourn, or feast, so that his very household becomes a visible warning of coming exile, though the chapter still promises an eventual regathering beyond it. Chapter 17 turns from Jeremiah's sign-acts to a broader meditation on trust, the deceitful heart, and Jerusalem's sabbath.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Told not to marry, mourn, or feast, so that his own restricted household life becomes a visible sign of the coming catastrophe (16:1-9).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Names persistent idolatry, generations deep, as the reason exile is coming, yet still promises an eventual regathering (16:10-15).

keyFigures.name: Judah's families
keyFigures.role: Warned that marriage, funerals, and feasts will cease in the land because of the coming judgment (16:1-9).

keyFigures.name: the nations
keyFigures.role: Promised that they will one day recognize the futility of the idols their ancestors inherited from their fathers (16:19-21).

keyThemes.explanation: Jeremiah's unmarried, childless, and solitary life becomes a living preview of a society where marriage, birth, and mourning are all about to stop (16:1-9).
Judah is said to have done worse than its fathers, each generation following its own stubborn heart instead of learning from the last (16:12).
The promise that people will one day swear by the LORD who brought Israel 'from the land of the north' describes a second exodus even bigger than the first (16:14-15).

Jeremiah 17.summary: Judah's sin is pictured as engraved deeply into the nation, while trust in human strength is contrasted with the lasting security of trusting the LORD (Jeremiah 17:1-8). The human heart is described as deceitful above all things, prompting Jeremiah's own prayer for healing (Jeremiah 17:9-14). A final sermon at Jerusalem's gates calls the city to honor the sabbath rather than carry on ordinary commerce, with blessing or judgment depending on the answer (Jeremiah 17:19-27).
Jeremiah 17.whereWeAre: Chapter 16 showed Jeremiah's restricted life acting out Judah's coming exile. Here the focus widens to the human heart itself, contrasting trust in human strength with trust in the LORD, before a closing sermon at Jerusalem's gates calls the city to honor the sabbath instead of ordinary commerce. Chapter 18 returns to acted-out prophecy at the potter's house, picturing God's freedom to reshape any nation's future.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Pictures Judah's sin as engraved with an iron pen and contrasts trust in human strength with the lasting security of trusting him (17:1, 17:5-8).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Describes the human heart as deceitful above all things and prays for his own healing from the LORD who searches it (17:9-10, 17:14).

keyFigures.name: people and kings of Judah
keyFigures.role: Addressed through Jeremiah's gate-sermon, with blessing or judgment set before them depending on whether they keep the sabbath (17:19-25).

keyFigures.name: Jerusalem's gate users
keyFigures.role: Ordinary traders and farmers warned to stop carrying loads and doing business on the sabbath (17:21-22).

keyThemes.explanation: The man who trusts in man is compared to a shrub in the desert, while the one who trusts the LORD is like a tree planted by water, unaffected even by drought (17:5-8).
Calling the heart 'deceitful above all things' warns that people, including Jeremiah himself, cannot fully trust their own self-assessment (17:9-10).
Keeping or breaking the sabbath is treated as a visible test of covenant loyalty with real consequences for Jerusalem's future (17:24-27).

Jeremiah 18.summary: God sends Jeremiah to watch a potter reshape spoiled clay, an image of his freedom to relent from judgment or withdraw a blessing depending on a nation's response (Jeremiah 18:1-10). Jerusalem's leaders reject this warning outright, insisting they will keep following their own devices regardless (Jeremiah 18:11-12). Opponents then plot against Jeremiah himself, prompting his anguished prayer that God remember how he stood in the breach for them (Jeremiah 18:18-23).
Jeremiah 18.whereWeAre: Chapter 17 closed with a sermon calling Jerusalem to honor the sabbath. Here God sends Jeremiah to watch a potter reworking flawed clay, a picture of his freedom to relent or to judge depending on a nation's response, and opponents respond to this message by plotting against the prophet himself. Chapter 19 takes the potter's image further, as Jeremiah breaks a finished jar beyond repair to show that Jerusalem's coming judgment cannot be reshaped away.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Shows Jeremiah a potter reworking flawed clay, a picture of his freedom to relent from judgment or withdraw blessing depending on a nation's response (18:1-10).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Delivers this warning faithfully, then prays in anguish after opponents plot against him for it (18:11, 18:19-23).

keyFigures.name: the potter
keyFigures.role: Reshapes a marred vessel on the wheel into a new one, exactly as it seems good to him (18:3-4).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah's opponents
keyFigures.role: Plan to attack Jeremiah 'with the tongue' rather than heed his warning, confident that priests and wise men will always be available (18:18).

keyThemes.explanation: A flawed pot reworked into a new one in the potter's own hands pictures God's freedom to reshape his plans for a nation rather than being bound to one fixed outcome (18:3-6).
Both warnings of judgment and promises of blessing are described as changeable, depending on whether a nation turns from evil or from good (18:7-10).
Opponents who plot against Jeremiah still expect priests, the wise, and prophets to keep functioning as usual, showing how unwilling they are to imagine life without those institutions (18:18).

Jeremiah 19.summary: God sends Jeremiah to buy a potter's earthen jar and gather elders and priests at the Valley of Hinnom to hear a message of judgment (Jeremiah 19:1-9). He denounces the bloodshed and idolatrous worship carried out at Topheth, including child sacrifice (Jeremiah 19:4-6). Breaking the jar before them signals that Jerusalem's coming destruction, unlike reworkable wet clay, cannot now be undone (Jeremiah 19:10-15).
Jeremiah 19.whereWeAre: Chapter 18 pictured clay that could still be reworked while soft. Here Jeremiah buys a finished pottery jar instead and breaks it before the elders and priests at Topheth, showing that Jerusalem's judgment, like fired clay, can no longer be undone. Chapter 20 shows the cost of that broken-jar sermon landing on Jeremiah personally, as the priest Pashhur has him beaten and put in the stocks.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends Jeremiah to buy a potter's jar and break it before elders and priests as a sign that Jerusalem's coming destruction cannot be undone (19:1-11).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Carries out the sign-act at the Valley of Hinnom and denounces the bloodshed and child sacrifice practiced there (19:1-6).

keyFigures.name: elders and priests
keyFigures.role: Summoned as official witnesses to watch Jeremiah break the jar and hear the judgment it represents (19:1-2, 19:10).

keyFigures.name: Judah's people
keyFigures.role: Condemned for filling Topheth with innocent blood and for worship that God says never entered his mind to command (19:4-5).

keyThemes.explanation: Breaking a finished, fired jar rather than reshaping wet clay marks the difference between a warning that can still be averted and one that cannot (19:10-11).
Topheth is renamed 'the valley of slaughter' because the bloodshed committed there will be answered with bloodshed in return (19:6).
Delivering this sign in front of elders and priests ensures the judgment is witnessed officially, not just spoken in private (19:1-2).

Jeremiah 20.summary: The priest-official Pashhur has Jeremiah beaten and locked in the stocks for his temple prophecy (Jeremiah 20:1-2). Released the next day, Jeremiah announces judgment on Pashhur by name and reframes his own ordeal as the costly burden of speaking God's word faithfully (Jeremiah 20:3-6). The chapter ends with Jeremiah's rawest lament, torn between an inner fire that compels him to speak and a despair deep enough to curse the day of his birth (Jeremiah 20:7-18).
Jeremiah 20.whereWeAre: Chapter 19 ended with Jeremiah breaking a jar to announce Jerusalem's irreversible judgment. Here the priest-official Pashhur answers that sermon by beating Jeremiah and locking him in the stocks, and the prophet's own anguish spills out afterward in the book's rawest lament, including a wish that he had never been born. Chapter 21 turns from Jeremiah's private suffering to a formal, public exchange with King Zedekiah himself.

keyFigures.name: Pashhur son of Immer
keyFigures.role: The priest in charge of the temple who has Jeremiah beaten and locked in the stocks for his prophecy, and is renamed 'Magormissabib' in judgment (20:1-3).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Released from the stocks, announces judgment on Pashhur by name, then pours out the book's rawest lament over his own suffering (20:3-6, 20:14-18).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: The source of the fire shut up in Jeremiah's bones that he cannot hold back no matter how much he is mocked (20:9, 20:11).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah's persecutors
keyFigures.role: Those who watch for Jeremiah to stumble, hoping to take revenge on him for his warnings (20:10).

keyThemes.explanation: Jeremiah's beating and night in the stocks show that faithful prophecy can carry a direct physical price, not just social disapproval (20:1-2).
Describing God's word as 'a burning fire shut up in my bones' pictures a calling too strong to suppress even when Jeremiah wants to quit (20:9).
Cursing the day of his own birth shows the full weight of Jeremiah's suffering without softening or hiding it from the reader (20:14-18).

Jeremiah 21.summary: King Zedekiah sends envoys to Jeremiah during Babylon's siege, hoping for an encouraging answer like deliverances God gave in the past (Jeremiah 21:1-2). Jeremiah instead declares that God himself will fight against the city, and urges those who want to live to surrender to the besieging army (Jeremiah 21:3-10). The royal house is commanded to practice justice every morning, especially for the oppressed, or face the same fire-like judgment (Jeremiah 21:11-14).
Jeremiah 21.whereWeAre: Chapter 20 closed with Jeremiah's most anguished personal lament. Here the setting shifts to the royal court: King Zedekiah sends envoys hoping for an encouraging word as Babylon's army closes in, but Jeremiah instead urges surrender and calls the royal house to practice justice for the oppressed. Chapter 22 continues addressing Judah's kings directly, reviewing the fates of Jehoiakim's predecessor, himself, and his successor.

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah
keyFigures.role: Judah's last king, who sends envoys to Jeremiah hoping God will again drive back Babylon's army as in the past (21:1-2).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Answers that God himself will fight against the city, and urges anyone who wants to live to surrender to the besiegers (21:3-10).

keyFigures.name: Pashhur son of Malchiah
keyFigures.role: One of the two royal envoys Zedekiah sends to ask Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD (21:1).

keyFigures.name: Zephaniah the priest
keyFigures.role: The second envoy sent with Pashhur to seek Jeremiah's word from the LORD (21:1).

keyFigures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
keyFigures.role: King of Babylon, whose besieging army Jeremiah says God himself is directing against Jerusalem (21:4-7).

keyThemes.explanation: Jeremiah refuses to give Zedekiah the encouraging answer he hopes for, showing that true prophecy does not bend to what a leader wants to hear (21:2-7).
The choice set before the people, death in the city or life by surrender, insists that survival is still possible even within a judgment already decided (21:8-9).
The royal house is commanded to 'execute judgment in the morning,' linking the king's daily administration of justice directly to the city's fate (21:12).

Jeremiah 22.summary: Jeremiah confronts Judah's royal house with God's demand for justice and mercy toward the vulnerable, warning that the palace itself will become a ruin without it (Jeremiah 22:1-9). He addresses the fates of three kings by name: Shallum, taken to Egypt never to return; Jehoiakim, condemned for forcing unpaid labor to build a lavish palace; and Coniah, who will be cast off and leave for exile (Jeremiah 22:10-30). The chapter contrasts this royal failure with Josiah's example of judging the cause of the poor and needy (Jeremiah 22:15-16).
Jeremiah 22.whereWeAre: Chapter 21 warned Zedekiah that resistance to Babylon would fail. Here Jeremiah reviews Judah's recent kings by name, demanding justice and mercy from the royal house and condemning Jehoiakim's exploitative building projects, while pronouncing that Jehoiachin will leave for exile and never return. Chapter 23 answers this record of failed kings with the promise of a different kind of ruler, a righteous Branch from David's line.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Confronts Judah's royal house at the king's house itself, demanding justice and mercy toward the vulnerable (22:1-5).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Warns that the palace will become a ruin without justice, and pronounces the fates of three kings in turn (22:5-30).

keyFigures.name: Shallum (Jehoahaz)
keyFigures.role: Josiah's son, taken captive to Egypt and told he will never see his native land again (22:10-12).

keyFigures.name: Jehoiakim
keyFigures.role: Condemned for building a lavish palace with unpaid labor and promised a burial fit for a donkey, dragged out beyond the gates (22:13-19).

keyFigures.name: Coniah (Jehoiachin)
keyFigures.role: Told that though he were the signet ring on God's own hand, he would still be pulled off and sent into exile childless on the throne (22:24-30).

keyThemes.explanation: Jehoiakim's cedar-paneled palace built with unpaid labor is condemned precisely because comfort was bought at someone else's unjust expense (22:13-14).
Three kings in a row are named and judged individually, showing that royal office does not exempt a ruler from personal accountability (22:11-12, 22:18-19, 22:24-27).
Josiah's example of judging 'the cause of the poor and needy' is called the true meaning of knowing God, redefining kingship around justice rather than splendor (22:15-16).

Jeremiah 23.summary: God condemns the shepherds, Judah's kings, who have scattered rather than cared for his flock, and promises to gather the remnant himself (Jeremiah 23:1-4). A righteous Branch from David is announced, a king who will reign wisely and bear the name 'THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS' (Jeremiah 23:5-6). The chapter then turns to extended warnings against prophets whose invented dreams and borrowed words mislead the people, contrasted with God's true word, like fire and a hammer breaking rock (Jeremiah 23:16-32).
Jeremiah 23.whereWeAre: Chapter 22 closed naming Judah's recent kings as failures who exploited rather than protected their people. Here God condemns the shepherds who scattered the flock and promises a righteous Branch from David instead, before turning to the false prophets whose comforting dreams and borrowed words mislead the very people they claim to serve. Chapter 24 moves from these warnings about false voices to a vision clarifying who actually carries hope after the first deportation.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Condemns the shepherds who scattered his flock and promises to gather the remnant himself under a righteous Branch from David (23:1-6).

keyFigures.name: Israel's and Judah's shepherds
keyFigures.role: The kings and leaders of both kingdoms, pictured as shepherds who destroyed and scattered rather than cared for God's flock (23:1-2).

keyFigures.name: future Davidic ruler
keyFigures.role: A righteous Branch who will reign wisely and bear the name 'THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS' (23:5-6).

keyFigures.name: false prophets
keyFigures.role: Share invented dreams and borrowed words as if they were God's own, contrasted with his true word, like fire and a hammer breaking rock (23:16, 23:25-29).

keyThemes.explanation: Kings who were meant to care for God's flock are condemned instead for destroying and scattering it, inverting their own job description (23:1-2).
The righteous Branch's name, 'THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS,' answers the failed kings of chapter 22 with the promise of a ruler who embodies the justice they lacked (23:5-6).
God's word is compared to fire and a hammer breaking rock, a built-in test for telling real prophecy apart from borrowed dreams and invented messages (23:28-29).

Jeremiah 24.summary: After King Jehoiachin's deportation to Babylon, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs set before the temple (Jeremiah 24:1-3). The exiles already carried to Babylon are compared to good figs, promised a future heart to know the LORD and an eventual return (Jeremiah 24:4-7). Those remaining under Zedekiah or fleeing to Egypt are compared instead to figs too rotten to eat, destined for further disaster (Jeremiah 24:8-10).
Jeremiah 24.whereWeAre: Chapter 23 warned against false prophets who mislead with empty comfort. Here, after Jehoiachin's exiles have already been deported to Babylon, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs and overturns easy assumptions: the exiles already in Babylon are the good figs with a future, while those remaining under Zedekiah are the bad figs headed for disaster. Chapter 25 widens this same reversal into a dated, formal review of twenty-three years of ignored warnings.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs and overturns easy assumptions about who is truly blessed after Jehoiachin's deportation (24:1-10).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Receives and explains the vision, naming the exiles already in Babylon as the ones with a future hope (24:3-7).

keyFigures.name: Jehoiachin's exiles
keyFigures.role: Compared to good figs, promised a new heart to know the LORD and an eventual return to the land (24:5-7).

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah and Judah's remnant
keyFigures.role: Compared instead to rotten figs, destined for further disaster whether they stay in Jerusalem or flee to Egypt (24:8-10).

keyThemes.explanation: Being carried off to Babylon is reinterpreted as the path to a new heart to know the LORD, reversing the assumption that exile is simply loss (24:5-7).
The same event, deportation to Babylon, is read as either disaster or hidden blessing depending on which basket of figs a person's situation resembles (24:1-10).
Staying in Jerusalem, which looks like the safer choice, turns out to be the one that leads to further disaster (24:8-10).

Jeremiah 25.summary: In Jehoiakim's fourth year, Jeremiah reviews twenty-three years of warnings that Judah has refused to hear despite his rising early to speak (Jeremiah 25:1-7). He announces that Babylon will devastate the land and that these nations will serve Babylon for seventy years, after which Babylon itself will be judged in turn (Jeremiah 25:8-14). Jeremiah is told to make many nations drink a cup of God's wrath, a judgment that reaches from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth (Jeremiah 25:15-29).
Jeremiah 25.whereWeAre: Chapter 24 pictured the Babylonian exiles, not those who stayed, as the ones with real hope. Here, in Jehoiakim's fourth year, Jeremiah reviews twenty-three years of warnings Judah refused to hear, announces Babylonian conquest followed by seventy years of service, and extends a cup of God's wrath to many nations beyond Judah. Chapter 26 shows what it actually cost Jeremiah to deliver a related message in public: a trial for his life at the temple.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Reviews twenty-three years of warnings Judah has refused to hear, from Josiah's thirteenth year to Jehoiakim's fourth (25:1-7).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Announces Babylonian conquest followed by seventy years of service, after which Babylon itself will be judged (25:8-14).

keyFigures.name: Jehoiakim
keyFigures.role: The king in whose fourth year this dated oracle is delivered, as Nebuchadnezzar's own reign begins (25:1, 25:3).

keyFigures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
keyFigures.role: Named 'my servant,' the instrument God will use to devastate Judah and the surrounding nations (25:9).

keyFigures.name: many nations
keyFigures.role: Made to drink the cup of God's wrath in turn, from Jerusalem outward to Egypt, Philistia, Edom, Moab, Ammon, and beyond (25:15-26).

keyThemes.explanation: Twenty-three years of 'rising early and speaking' without being heard shows how long patience can be extended before judgment finally arrives (25:3-4).
Fixing Babylon's rule at seventy years builds an expiration date into Judah's punishment from the very start of the sentence (25:11-12).
The cup of wrath passed from nation to nation shows that God's justice is not limited to Judah but reaches every people in turn (25:17-26).

Jeremiah 26.summary: Early in Jehoiakim's reign, Jeremiah preaches at the temple that it could become like ruined Shiloh if the people do not turn back, and priests and prophets seize him and demand his execution (Jeremiah 26:1-11). Jeremiah defends his mission before the officials, and elders recall that the earlier prophet Micah gave a similar warning in Hezekiah's day without being put to death (Jeremiah 26:12-19). The chapter also records the fate of another prophet, Uriah, extradited from Egypt and killed by Jehoiakim, showing how real the danger was that spared Jeremiah through Ahikam's protection (Jeremiah 26:20-24).
Jeremiah 26.whereWeAre: Chapter 25 pronounced judgment on many nations from a safe distance of years. Here that same kind of warning, delivered face to face at the temple, nearly gets Jeremiah killed; elders defend him by recalling the earlier prophet Micah, though another prophet, Uriah, is extradited and executed for saying much the same thing. Chapter 27 shows Jeremiah facing down a similar danger, this time by wearing a yoke to warn Judah and its neighbors against resisting Babylon.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Preaches at the temple that it could become like ruined Shiloh, then defends his mission before officials demanding his death (26:1-15).

keyFigures.name: Jehoiakim
keyFigures.role: The king under whom this trial takes place, and who later kills the prophet Uriah for the same kind of message (26:1, 26:20-23).

keyFigures.name: priests and prophets
keyFigures.role: Seize Jeremiah after his sermon and insist to the officials that he deserves to die (26:7-11).

keyFigures.name: elders and officials
keyFigures.role: Side with Jeremiah, recalling that the earlier prophet Micah gave Hezekiah a similar warning without being executed (26:16-19).

keyFigures.name: Uriah
keyFigures.role: Another prophet who preached the same message, fled to Egypt, and was extradited and killed by Jehoiakim (26:20-23).

keyFigures.name: Ahikam
keyFigures.role: The son of Shaphan whose protection keeps Jeremiah from being handed over to the people to be put to death (26:24).

keyThemes.explanation: Jeremiah is specifically told to speak 'all the words' without diminishing anything, even knowing how dangerous the full message will be (26:2).
A formal trial over Jeremiah's words puts prophecy itself on public trial, deciding through due process whether his claim to speak for God is genuine (26:10-16).
Uriah's extradition and execution for a nearly identical message shows concretely what could have happened to Jeremiah without Ahikam's protection (26:20-24).

Jeremiah 27.summary: Jeremiah wears a wooden yoke and urges Judah, along with envoys from several neighboring nations, to accept Babylonian rule rather than trust predictions of swift freedom (Jeremiah 27:1-11). He warns Zedekiah directly that submission, not resistance, will preserve his life and the city (Jeremiah 27:12-15). He also tells the priests and people that the temple vessels will remain under Babylon's control, contradicting prophets who promised their quick return (Jeremiah 27:16-22).
Jeremiah 27.whereWeAre: Chapter 26 showed Jeremiah barely surviving a death sentence for his temple warning. Here he risks confrontation again, wearing a wooden yoke to urge Judah and the envoys of neighboring nations to accept Babylonian rule rather than trust predictions of quick freedom. Chapter 28 shows exactly that kind of false prediction arriving publicly, as the prophet Hananiah breaks Jeremiah's yoke before the watching crowd.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Wears a wooden yoke and sends word to Judah and neighboring kings urging submission to Babylon rather than trust in quick freedom (27:1-11).

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah
keyFigures.role: Told directly that serving the king of Babylon, not resisting him, is the way to live (27:12-15).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Claims to have given all these lands to Nebuchadnezzar and warns that the temple vessels will remain under Babylon's control (27:5-8, 27:16-22).

keyFigures.name: envoys of neighboring kings
keyFigures.role: Ambassadors from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon who come to Jerusalem, apparently planning a joint revolt against Babylon (27:3).

keyFigures.name: false prophets
keyFigures.role: Promise the temple vessels will soon return, a claim Jeremiah flatly contradicts (27:16).

keyThemes.explanation: Wearing an actual wooden yoke turns Jeremiah's message into something onlookers can see as well as hear, reinforcing submission to Babylon as the unavoidable near-term reality (27:2-3).
Zedekiah is warned specifically not to listen to prophets promising he will not serve Babylon, since that comfort is false (27:14-15).
Submitting to Babylon's yoke, rather than resisting it, is presented as the path that actually preserves the nation rather than destroying it (27:11-12).

Jeremiah 28.summary: In the temple, the prophet Hananiah announces that Babylon's yoke will soon break and that exiles and temple objects will return within two years (Jeremiah 28:1-4). He breaks the wooden yoke from Jeremiah's neck as a dramatic sign of his claim (Jeremiah 28:10-11). Jeremiah answers that an iron yoke will replace it and predicts Hananiah's death within the year, which the chapter reports happening two months later (Jeremiah 28:12-17).
Jeremiah 28.whereWeAre: Chapter 27 had Jeremiah wear a yoke as a sign of submission to Babylon. Here the prophet Hananiah publicly breaks that yoke and promises a two-year deliverance, so Jeremiah answers with an iron yoke and a prediction of Hananiah's own death within the year, which the chapter reports happening. Chapter 29 takes this same conflict over false hope to the exiles already living in Babylon.

keyFigures.name: Hananiah son of Azzur
keyFigures.role: A prophet who publicly breaks Jeremiah's yoke and promises Babylon's rule will end within two years (28:1-4, 28:10-11).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Answers that an iron yoke will replace the broken wooden one and predicts Hananiah's death within the year (28:12-16).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Confirms Jeremiah's word by causing Hananiah to die two months later, exactly as announced (28:16-17).

keyFigures.name: priests and people
keyFigures.role: Gathered in the temple to witness the public contest between Jeremiah's and Hananiah's conflicting claims (28:1, 28:5).

keyThemes.explanation: Hananiah and Jeremiah deliver opposite messages in the same temple courtyard, forcing onlookers to decide which prophet actually speaks for God (28:1-11).
Breaking Jeremiah's wooden yoke is answered with the announcement of an iron one, showing that a dramatic gesture does not by itself make a prophecy true (28:10-14).
Hananiah's death within the year he predicted shows that claiming to speak for God carries real consequences when the claim turns out false (28:16-17).

Jeremiah 29.summary: Jeremiah writes to the exiles already deported to Babylon, telling them to build houses, plant gardens, marry, and seek the peace of the city where they now live rather than wait on false hopes of quick return (Jeremiah 29:1-9). He promises that after seventy years God will fulfill his good word toward them, including the well-known assurance of 'thoughts of peace, and not of evil' (Jeremiah 29:10-14). A conflict with the false prophet Shemaiah shows that disagreement over Jeremiah's message continues even among the exiles themselves (Jeremiah 29:24-32).
Jeremiah 29.whereWeAre: Chapter 28 showed a false prophet's promise of quick deliverance collapsing within the year. Here Jeremiah writes directly to the exiles already in Babylon, telling them to build houses, plant gardens, and seek their captors' peace rather than wait for a rescue Hananiah's kind keeps promising, while still holding out hope for an eventual return. Chapters 30 and 31 open the book's fullest promises of restoration, the oracles the exiles were told to wait for.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Writes to the exiles in Babylon, telling them to build houses, plant gardens, and seek their captors' peace while waiting for God's promised return (29:1-9).

keyFigures.name: the exiles
keyFigures.role: The first deportees in Babylon, told to settle in for the long term rather than expect an immediate rescue (29:4-7).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Promises that after seventy years he will fulfill his good word toward the exiles, including 'thoughts of peace, and not of evil' (29:10-11).

keyFigures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
keyFigures.role: King of Babylon, who carried this first wave of exiles away and under whose rule they are told to seek their new city's peace (29:1-3, 29:7).

keyFigures.name: Shemaiah
keyFigures.role: An exile in Babylon who opposes Jeremiah's letter and is condemned for prophesying falsely in the LORD's name (29:24-32).

keyFigures.name: Elnathan and Gemariah
keyFigures.role: Royal officials who carry Jeremiah's letter to the exiles in Babylon (29:3).

keyThemes.explanation: Telling the exiles to build houses and plant gardens rather than wait anxiously calls them to live fully even in an unwanted, temporary-feeling situation (29:5-7).
The promise of 'an expected end' after seventy years gives the exiles a horizon to hope toward without pretending the wait will be short (29:10-11).
Shemaiah's opposition from within Babylon shows that even exiled communities still had to sort true guidance from false (29:24-32).

Jeremiah 30.summary: God directs Jeremiah to write down promises of restoration so that the words will last (Jeremiah 30:1-3). The chapter describes a terrifying time of anguish, 'the time of Jacob's trouble,' from which God still promises to save his people (Jeremiah 30:4-11). It closes with healing after discipline, relief from foreign oppression, and the people restored once more to covenant belonging (Jeremiah 30:12-22).
Jeremiah 30.whereWeAre: Chapter 29 told the exiles to settle into Babylon while still trusting a future return. Here that future arrives in writing: God tells Jeremiah to record promises of healing, regathering, and relief from foreign oppression, even naming the coming crisis 'the time of Jacob's trouble' from which his people will still be saved. Chapter 31 continues this same promise of restoration, reaching its high point in a new covenant written on the heart.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Directs Jeremiah to record promises of restoration and describes a terrifying 'time of Jacob's trouble' from which his people will still be saved (30:1-7).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Receives and writes down these promises of healing and regathering for a future readership (30:2).

keyFigures.name: Israel and Judah
keyFigures.role: Promised relief from foreign oppression, healing from their wounds, and restoration to covenant belonging (30:3, 30:17, 30:22).

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: Invoked as the nation's ancestral name in the promise that his tents will be restored and his dwelling places pitied (30:18).

keyThemes.explanation: Naming the coming anguish 'the time of Jacob's trouble' does not minimize how bad it will be, even while promising rescue out of it (30:7).
God promises to heal wounds that others call incurable, directly answering the despair of a nation that assumes its situation cannot improve (30:12-13, 30:17).
Restored leadership 'from the midst of them' pictures a community governed again by its own people rather than foreign rule (30:20-21).

Jeremiah 31.summary: God promises restoration to Israel and Judah with images of renewed joy, planting, and a homecoming so real that it answers even the ancestral grief pictured in Rachel weeping for her children (Jeremiah 31:1-20). The chapter's center is a new covenant in which God's instruction is written on hearts rather than tablets of stone, and sins are forgiven and remembered no more (Jeremiah 31:31-34). It closes picturing Jerusalem itself rebuilt and measured out securely, never again to be uprooted (Jeremiah 31:38-40).
Jeremiah 31.whereWeAre: Chapter 30 opened the Book of Consolation with promises of healing and regathering. Here that hope reaches its height: Israel and Judah are promised joy, planting, and a homecoming so real that even Rachel's poetic grief is answered, and God announces a new covenant in which his instruction is written on hearts rather than stone. Chapter 32 grounds this same hope in an ordinary, costly transaction: Jeremiah buying a field while Jerusalem is under siege.

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Promises Israel and Judah renewed joy and planting, answers Rachel's grief with hope, and announces a new covenant written on the heart (31:1-20, 31:31-34).

keyFigures.name: Israel (Ephraim)
keyFigures.role: Addressed as a dear son whom God still remembers with mercy despite its wandering (31:9, 31:20).

keyFigures.name: Judah
keyFigures.role: Promised its own homecoming alongside Israel's, pictured as virgins dancing again with instruments of joy (31:4, 31:23).

keyFigures.name: Rachel
keyFigures.role: Pictured weeping for her exiled children, a grief God answers with the promise that they will return (31:15-17).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: The prophetic voice through whom these restoration promises, including the new covenant, are delivered (31:1).

keyThemes.explanation: Promising dancing, planting, and a homecoming so complete it answers Rachel's grief turns abstract hope into vivid, everyday pictures of restored life (31:4-5, 31:15-17).
Writing God's law on hearts instead of tablets addresses the Law's own weakness, a covenant people kept breaking from the outside in (31:31-33).
Measuring out the rebuilt city's boundaries turns restoration from a vague promise into a concrete, surveyed reality (31:38-40).

explainedReferences.explanation: Promise to write his law on his people's hearts and minds.
The new covenant's law written on hearts and forgiveness.
Promise to remember their sins and iniquities no more.

Jeremiah 32.summary: During Jerusalem's siege, with Jeremiah himself imprisoned, God tells him that his cousin Hanamel will offer to sell him a field at Anathoth, and Jeremiah buys it even though the land is about to fall to Babylon (Jeremiah 32:1-15). Documents are signed, sealed, and stored in an earthen jar before witnesses, a sign that houses, fields, and vineyards will be possessed again in the land (Jeremiah 32:9-15). Jeremiah prays for understanding, and God answers by explaining both why Jerusalem must fall and how he will restore it afterward through an everlasting covenant (Jeremiah 32:36-44).
Jeremiah 32.whereWeAre: Chapter 31 promised a new covenant written on the heart. Here that promise is acted out in a very practical way: during Jerusalem's siege, with Jeremiah himself imprisoned, he buys his cousin's field at Anathoth and has the deed sealed and stored as a sign that houses and fields will be owned again in the land. Chapter 33 continues this same promise of future normal life while Jeremiah remains confined.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Imprisoned during the siege, buys his cousin's field at Anathoth as a sign that property will be owned again in the land (32:1-15).

keyFigures.name: Hanamel
keyFigures.role: Jeremiah's cousin, whose offer to sell his field becomes the occasion for this sign of future hope (32:6-9).

keyFigures.name: Baruch
keyFigures.role: Receives the sealed and open copies of the deed to store in an earthen jar so they will last a long time (32:12-14).

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah
keyFigures.role: The king under whose siege of Jerusalem this purchase takes place, with Jeremiah confined in his court (32:1-5).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Explains why Jerusalem must fall for its persistent wrongdoing, yet promises an everlasting covenant of restoration afterward (32:26-42).

keyFigures.name: witnesses
keyFigures.role: Those who sign the deed of purchase according to the law and custom of the land (32:10, 32:12).

keyThemes.explanation: Buying a field about to fall to Babylon only makes sense as an act of faith that the land will belong to God's people again (32:7-9, 32:15).
God recounts how Israel and Judah 'have only done evil before me from their youth' since he brought them out of Egypt, explaining why judgment, not just bad luck, has arrived (32:20-21, 32:30).
The same chapter that explains Jerusalem's fall also promises an everlasting covenant afterward, holding judgment and hope together rather than choosing one (32:36-41).

Jeremiah 33.summary: While Jeremiah is still confined in the court of the prison, God again promises the restoration of Judah and Jerusalem, including healing, forgiveness, and renewed celebration (Jeremiah 33:1-11). He promises that the Davidic throne and the Levitical priesthood will continue, as reliable as the fixed cycle of day and night (Jeremiah 33:14-22). Some portions of the chapter are preserved only in the longer Hebrew textual tradition, a reminder that the book's transmission has its own history (Jeremiah 33:14-26).
Jeremiah 33.whereWeAre: Chapter 32 enacted hope through the purchase of a field during siege. Here, still shut up in the court of the prison, Jeremiah receives further promises of healing, forgiveness, celebration, and renewal for both the Davidic throne and the priestly line, pictured as reliable as day following night. Chapter 34 turns from these promises back to the present siege, where a very different test of faithfulness is unfolding.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Still confined in the court of the prison, receives further promises of healing, forgiveness, and renewal for Jerusalem (33:1-9).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Invites Jeremiah to call on him and promises the Davidic throne and Levitical priesthood will endure as surely as day and night (33:3, 33:19-22).

keyFigures.name: Davidic rulers
keyFigures.role: Promised an unbroken line to sit on David's throne despite the coming exile (33:17, 33:21).

keyFigures.name: Levitical priests
keyFigures.role: Promised their ministry before God will continue without end, paired with David's throne in this promise (33:18, 33:21).

keyFigures.name: Judah and Israel
keyFigures.role: Promised celebration, healing, and cleansing from the very sins that brought on their present judgment (33:7-9).

keyThemes.explanation: God promises to heal and reveal 'great and mighty things' to a city already marked for destruction, refusing to let its coming ruin be the final word (33:3, 33:6-9).
The sounds of joy, gladness, and thanksgiving returning to ruined streets reverses the images of silence and desolation used earlier in the book (33:10-11).
Comparing God's covenant with David to the fixed cycle of day and night makes the promise's reliability as certain as the most basic fact of nature (33:20-21).

Jeremiah 34.summary: As Babylon attacks, Jeremiah tells Zedekiah plainly that Jerusalem will fall and that he will be taken captive to Babylon, though he will die in peace (Jeremiah 34:1-7). A covenant to free Hebrew slaves is made during the siege but then broken when former owners force the freed people back into slavery (Jeremiah 34:8-11). The LORD condemns this reversal as a betrayal of both liberty and covenant, promising the very 'liberty' of sword, pestilence, and famine instead (Jeremiah 34:12-22).
Jeremiah 34.whereWeAre: Chapter 33 promised that David's line and the priestly line would endure as surely as day and night. Here that same test of faithfulness plays out in the present: as Babylon attacks, Judah's leaders free their Hebrew slaves under covenant and then violently take them back, a betrayal God condemns in the strongest terms. Chapter 35 contrasts this broken covenant with a very different family's quiet, generations-long faithfulness.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Tells Zedekiah plainly that Jerusalem will fall and that he will be taken to Babylon, though he will die in peace (34:1-7).

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah
keyFigures.role: Warned of his personal fate as Babylon's army closes in on Jerusalem's last fortified cities (34:2-5).

keyFigures.name: Judah's slaveowners
keyFigures.role: Make and then break a covenant to free their Hebrew slaves, re-enslaving them once Babylon's siege briefly lifts (34:8-11).

keyFigures.name: freed Hebrew slaves
keyFigures.role: Released under covenant law, only to be forced back into service by their former owners (34:10-11).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Condemns the broken covenant as a betrayal of both liberty and his own name, announcing a different 'liberty,' to sword, famine, and plague (34:15-17).

keyThemes.explanation: Jeremiah tells Zedekiah his exact fate in advance, refusing to soften the news even though it is addressed directly to the king himself (34:2-5).
Freeing slaves and then forcing them back profanes God's name specifically because it treats a covenant made in his name as disposable (34:15-16).
The announced 'liberty' of sword, famine, and plague mirrors the liberty the people refused to give, making the punishment match the crime (34:17).

Jeremiah 35.summary: Jeremiah brings the Rechabite family into the temple and sets wine before them, which they refuse because their ancestor Jonadab commanded a disciplined life free of wine and permanent houses generations earlier (Jeremiah 35:1-11). God contrasts their lasting obedience to a human command with Judah's refusal to heed warning after warning from him directly (Jeremiah 35:12-16). He promises the Rechabites an enduring place in his service as a rebuke to Judah's unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 35:18-19).
Jeremiah 35.whereWeAre: Chapter 34 condemned Judah for breaking its covenant to free Hebrew slaves. Here the Rechabites model the opposite: brought into the temple and offered wine, they refuse because their ancestor commanded a simple, disciplined way of life generations earlier, and God holds up their loyalty to shame Judah's refusal to heed his own repeated warnings. Chapter 36 returns to Jeremiah's own struggle to be heard, as his written words face a king's direct hostility.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Brings the Rechabite family into the temple and sets wine before them as a test of their loyalty to their ancestor's command (35:1-5).

keyFigures.name: Rechabites
keyFigures.role: Refuse the wine because their ancestor Jonadab commanded a life without wine or permanent houses, a command they have kept for generations (35:6-10).

keyFigures.name: Jaazaniah
keyFigures.role: The Rechabite leader who answers Jeremiah and explains the family's reason for refusing the wine (35:3, 35:6).

keyFigures.name: Jonadab son of Rechab
keyFigures.role: The ancestor whose command, given generations earlier, the Rechabites still keep without exception (35:6-10).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Contrasts the Rechabites' lasting obedience with Judah's refusal to heed his own prophets, and promises Jonadab's line an enduring place before him (35:12-16, 35:18-19).

keyThemes.explanation: The Rechabites' generations-long obedience to a human ancestor's command, with no exceptions even under pressure, sets an unusually high bar for consistency (35:8-10).
God contrasts how readily the Rechabites obeyed Jonadab with how little Judah has obeyed him, 'rising early and speaking' through prophet after prophet (35:14-15).
Promising Jonadab's descendants an enduring place before God rewards faithfulness that had nothing to do with Israel's covenant in the first place (35:18-19).

Jeremiah 36.summary: In Jehoiakim's reign, Jeremiah dictates all his messages since Josiah's day to Baruch, who writes them on a scroll and reads them publicly at the temple (Jeremiah 36:1-10). Officials bring the scroll to the king, who cuts it apart and burns it piece by piece despite pleas to stop (Jeremiah 36:20-26). Jeremiah dictates another scroll with the same words and more besides, showing that the king's violence could destroy paper but not the message itself (Jeremiah 36:27-32).
Jeremiah 36.whereWeAre: Chapter 35 held up the Rechabites' quiet obedience against Judah's refusal to listen. Here Jeremiah's own warnings reach their most dramatic rejection: Baruch writes them on a scroll and reads them publicly, but King Jehoiakim cuts the scroll apart and burns it, only for Jeremiah to dictate it again with more added. Chapter 37 shows Jeremiah's message facing renewed danger under a different king, Zedekiah, as the Babylonian siege itself briefly lifts.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Dictates all his messages since Josiah's day to Baruch, intending the scroll to be read publicly in hope the people will still turn back (36:1-7).

keyFigures.name: Baruch
keyFigures.role: Writes the scroll at Jeremiah's dictation and reads it aloud at the temple, then rewrites it after the king destroys the first copy (36:4, 36:32).

keyFigures.name: Jehoiakim
keyFigures.role: Cuts the scroll apart with a penknife and burns it in his winter house despite officials' pleas to stop (36:22-25).

keyFigures.name: Gemariah and court officials
keyFigures.role: Hear the scroll read, grow afraid, and try unsuccessfully to keep the king from burning it (36:11-12, 36:25).

keyFigures.name: the LORD
keyFigures.role: Hides Jeremiah and Baruch from arrest and commands the scroll to be rewritten with additional words of judgment against Jehoiakim (36:26-31).

keyThemes.explanation: Recording the prophecies on a scroll preserves Jeremiah's entire ministry in one place, so that even officials who missed the original messages can still hear them (36:2-4).
Jehoiakim's calm destruction of the scroll, cutting and burning it piece by piece without fear, shows contempt that goes beyond simple disagreement (36:23-24).
Dictating the scroll again so that 'there were added besides unto them many like words' shows that destroying a physical copy cannot actually undo a message once it has been spoken (36:28, 36:32).

Jeremiah 37.summary: Zedekiah seeks Jeremiah's prayer as Babylon's siege temporarily lifts before an advancing Egyptian army (Jeremiah 37:1-5). Jeremiah insists Babylon will return and destroy the city regardless, a message so unwelcome that he is accused of deserting to the enemy and imprisoned (Jeremiah 37:11-15). Zedekiah later moves him to the court of the guard, where he receives bread daily until the city's food runs out (Jeremiah 37:17-21).
Jeremiah 37.whereWeAre: Chapter 36 showed a king's violence unable to destroy Jeremiah's written word. Here Zedekiah seeks Jeremiah's prayer as Babylon's army temporarily withdraws before an Egyptian advance, but Jeremiah insists Babylon will return, and his honesty earns him imprisonment on a false charge of desertion. Chapter 38 shows that imprisonment grow even more dangerous, as officials lower Jeremiah into a muddy cistern to silence him for good.

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah
keyFigures.role: Seeks Jeremiah's prayer as Babylon's siege lifts temporarily before an advancing Egyptian army (37:1-3).

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.role: Insists Babylon will return and destroy the city, and is arrested as a deserter when he tries to leave for his own territory (37:6-15).

keyFigures.name: Irijah
keyFigures.role: The guard who arrests Jeremiah at the gate, accusing him of deserting to the Babylonians (37:13-14).
